queue.opening: It’s Monday, November 16. This is The Front Page , your daily window into the world of The Free Press —and our take on the world at large. Today: Eli Lake on the Democrats’ showdown over who will lead the Senate. Jed Rubenfeld on the strange case of Ilhan Omar. Coleman Hughes interviews Ben Shapiro. And much more. But first: How much is one CEO worth? On Sunday, the Financial Times reported that Jensen Huang and his allies were plotting his return as CEO of Nvidia, the giant chip maker he co-founded and ran until his resignation last week. On one level, the idea is—how to put this?—insane. Only last week, Huang stepped down after reports of three affairs—one with an alleged Chinese spy and two with women who reported to him at Nvidia—and is now being scrutinized (including by Matt Pottinger and Liza Tobin in these pages ) over allegations he worked to evade export controls on chips. How could Huang possibly do the job again? But consider a number: $570 billion. That’s how much Nvidia’s stock market value has dropped since the start of the scandal. It’s therefore arguably a crude measure of Huang’s value to the company. And, when faced with that many zeros, what are a few indiscretions? Or so the members of Nvidia’s board of directors might be asking themselves. queue.title: Pompeii home buried by Mount Vesuvius yields personal treasures untouched for nearly 2,000 years
queue.dek: A woman's cabinet sealed since Mount Vesuvius erupted in A.D. 79 held a children's amulet necklace, perfume bottle, bronze coins and makeup tools, archaeologists found.
queue.opening: Archaeologists excavating a home in ancient Pompeii recently uncovered the remains of an ancient Roman cabinet — revealing intimate belongings buried for nearly 2,000 years. The discovery was announced by Pompeii Archaeological Park. Officials said in a press release in late October, which was translated from Italian, that the cabinet was discovered in house IX 11, 7, also known as the House of Cornelius Maximus, along the Via dell'Abbondanza. HIDDEN UNDERGROUND CHAMBER REVEALED BENEATH HOME OF LEGENDARY ROMAN EMPEROR The cabinet — which officials believe belonged to a woman — had apparently remained unopened since Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 A.D. Using clues from the excavation, archaeologists were able to determine what the cabinet originally looked like and identify the belongings stored inside. Pictures released by officials show ancient pottery and other artifacts uncovered during the excavation. The cabinet contained tweezers, a tool for mixing makeup and a glass perfume bottle , as well as an incense burner, a bronze oil lamp and lead weights. SUNKEN ROYAL PALACE WITH CLEOPATRA LINK YIELDS RARE FIND TIED TO LONG-LOST WONDER OF ANCIENT WORLD Among the discoveries was a necklace made up of at least 24 miniature charms, including depictions of gods, hands, feet, pine cones and bunches of grapes. queue.title: I voted to open trade with China. 25 years later, it’s time for us to fix that mistake
queue.dek: Former senator who voted to grant China permanent normal trade relations now calls it the worst vote of his career and urges disengagement.
queue.opening: Twenty-five years ago, in December 2001, China officially joined the World Trade Organization (WTO) and fully entered the global economy. This was only possible because, a year earlier, the United States granted the communist country permanent normal trading relations status, granting China a level of access to our economy normally reserved for friends and allies like Great Britain and Israel. I was one of 83 senators who voted to do so. I now look back on it as the worst vote I made in 14 years in the Senate. Since that day, China has grown into an economic and military powerhouse. It has used that status malevolently, conducting genocides targeting Uyghurs, Tibetans and Falun Gong practitioners. It has organized an alliance of authoritarians to menace the free world, and it has empowered human rights abuses across the globe. It is now building up its nuclear weapons capacity to pair with a naval fleet now more numerous than our own. We believed — or deceived ourselves into believing — that a communist China engaged in the global economy would grow more open and free. We thought a China more exposed to the free world would be gravitationally attracted to freedom. Republicans haven’t fully lost rural America, but they got one heck of a warning. Just before the election, a national survey of rural voters found that about 75% rated their local cost of living as fair or poor. Nearly half worried about making their rent or mortgage payments. Meanwhile, family farm bankruptcies jumped 46% in 2025. queue.title: How America can win the AI race without burning voters

queue.opening: One of the biggest losers on Election Day was the AI industry. Across the country, voters delivered a clear warning about the rapid expansion of data centers powering artificial intelligence. Americans want technological progress, but not at the expense of their communities, electricity bills, water supplies or quality of life. According to Ballotpedia, 46 of the 47 data-center-related ballot measures decided in 2026 favored greater limits on development. The message is unmistakable: The industry is losing public confidence, and political leaders who ignore these concerns do so at their own peril. America needs more data centers, not fewer, to maintain its AI leadership. But technology companies cannot expect communities to welcome projects when residents believe they are absorbing the costs while corporations reap the benefits. queue.title: Chuck Schumer Won the Senate. Can He Keep His Job?
queue.dek: Until this year, it would have been hard to imagine him being punished for helping lead his party to a historic midterm election victory. A bid to unseat him shows the Democratic Party is changing, writes Eli Lake.
queue.opening: If you want to know just how far left the Democrats have traveled since their triumph in the midterms just two weeks ago, pay close attention to what happens to Senator Chuck Schumer. In most years, Schumer would be a lock for the powerful post of Senate majority leader, which he held from 2021 to 2025. As the minority leader in the past election cycle, he helped recruit and fund the candidates who have given his party a five-seat majority in the Senate, with the possibility of six depending on the outcome of the election in Alaska. And yet Schumer is facing an insurgent challenger, Chris Van Hollen , a Maryland senator who aligns with the progressive wing of his party. Since formally announcing his bid to be majority leader, Van Hollen has blasted Schumer for endorsing moderates in Senate primaries earlier this year. He has also threatened to shut down the federal government in order to defund the war in Iran. Van Hollen may not be likely to win. Unlike the House, the insurgent left is still nascent in the Senate with only a handful of committed members, including old-timer Bernie Sanders, newcomers such as Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and Troy Jackson of Maine, and sometime fellow travelers like Connecticut’s Chris Murphy. But the challenge to Schumer shows that Democrats’ rift over Israel wasn’t mere election fodder. queue.title: Tyler Cowen: How Much Is a CEO Worth? Ask Nvidia.
queue.dek: Nvidia lost $570 billion when its CEO resigned. The market’s slump after his exit reveals his failures—but also his value, writes Tyler Cowen.
queue.opening: How much is a CEO worth? As I am writing this column, the Nvidia share price has fallen by more than 12 percent since the allegations of Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy, followed by other allegations of affairs with women who work at Nvidia, and Huang’s subsequent exit from the company. That represents a value loss of about $570 billion, bringing the market capitalization of the company under $4 trillion. If we go back to October 6, the company has fallen in value by more than 30 percent since that date, or about $1.85 trillion. It’s no surprise that, despite everything, the Financial Times reported Sunday that Huang is considering a comeback, backed by his allies in Silicon Valley. We’ll have a better sense of Huang’s overall value to his company once more facts are in. If his indiscretions drag down the company in the long run, along with the sudden leadership change, that will count against him. And if he schemed to evade U.S. export controls, that would partly overshadow his contributions because of the importance of national security. But from a purely material standpoint, Huang excelled in co-founding Nvidia, driving its growth aggressively, and seeing how important it was to cultivate the AI sector as a whole to boost the demand for the company’s GPUs and other products. queue.opening: Doesn't anything work around here anymore? Oh sure, said Transportation chief Sean Duffy , it's just that all our crumbling equipment failed to communicate with our new equipment and this will take days to untangle. This has been a problem for years and will take $50 billion to fix. Did we forget to tell you? Two days earlier, Microsoft was so very sorry, but its Outlook email system imploded for 36 hours. Entire offices shut down because no one could get any work done, with employees unable to send messages and unaware of who was trying to reach them. OUTAGES RAISE CONCERN OVER CYBER VULNERABILITIES IN US The outages crippled governments, schools and businesses around the world. The software giant couldn't quite say what happened, first blaming its servers and then a "network capacity upgrade." But I suppose it fostered a feeling of togetherness, as if everyone was trapped in the same dark tunnel. We've all become accustomed to the frustrations of the digital world. I get 20 or more spam texts a day. I reflexively click on a button that says Stop and Delete Spam. queue.title: As US credit card debt hits $1.29T, bank algorithms are rejecting debt-free, six-figure earners
queue.dek: Across the country, debt-free Americans earning six figures face credit card denials as bank algorithms flag thin credit files as high-risk behavior.
queue.opening: Across the country, Americans earning six-figure salaries, carrying no debt and sitting on healthy savings accounts are increasingly hitting an unexpected wall when applying for everyday credit cards or loans: instant denial from automated bank algorithms. The rejections highlight a growing rift between kitchen-table financial discipline and corporate underwriting models. While nationwide credit card balances have climbed to a record $1.29 trillion — a 67% surge since early 2021, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York — data from the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) shows an estimated 25 million adults have credit files "too thin" or stale to generate a standard score. Rather than rewarding households that avoid borrowing, modern underwriting algorithms can interpret limited recent credit activity as a sign of uncertain lending risk, potentially making it harder for some debt-free consumers to qualify for credit. "Is corporate America penalizing people who live debt-free? I would say they're not penalizing them, but they are not prioritizing them because we're not the ones making them money," Jade Warshaw, co-host of "The Ramsey Show" — who paid off $460,000 in debt alongside her husband — told Fox News Digital. "When you think about the credit score in general, the whole purpose, it's a product, and so it's out there for banks to make money.
